builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Auditing a Learned Simulator for Legged Robots: The Robotic World Model on ANYmal D
summary: An end-to-end audit methodology for learned dynamics models, replacing the standard practice of validating world models with one-step-ahead error; it substitutes multi-step rollout evaluation, compression stress tests, uncertainty calibration checks, and policy-in-simulator testing. It costs substantial evaluation engineering (101 retrained simulators, 200 compressed copies, a hand-built MuJoCo model, policy training per simulator) rather than inference resources, though the authors note it ran without a GPU. It can fail to transfer because better one- and eight-step accuracy did not predict walking success (13 of 18 more accurate fine-tuned models produced failing policies), ensemble variance collapses under the implemented loss, and the scope is one robot, one gait, simulated data only.
rationale: The paper contributes audit methodology rather than a deployable component, and its robotics scope limits direct adoption, but its central lesson—long-horizon rollout evaluation can contradict one-step metrics—is directly testable for any team that trains predictors or dynamics models on a single GPU.
technique: Long-horizon audit of learned robot dynamics models

claims.statement: An end-to-end audit methodology for learned dynamics models, replacing the standard practice of validating world models with one-step-ahead error; it substitutes multi-step rollout evaluation, compression stress tests, uncertainty calibration checks, and policy-in-simulator testing. It costs substantial evaluation engineering (101 retrained simulators, 200 compressed copies, a hand-built MuJoCo model, policy training per simulator) rather than inference resources, though the authors note it ran without a GPU. It can fail to transfer because better one- and eight-step accuracy did not predict walking success (13 of 18 more accurate fine-tuned models produced failing policies), ensemble variance collapses under the implemented loss, and the scope is one robot, one gait, simulated data only.

Training on the model's own rollouts beat one-step training at 368 steps on all ten held-out episodes, while one-step metrics misranked designs (30% pruning kept 90% of skill one step ahead but 39% at 2 s); ensemble disagreement ranked rollout error at Spearman +0.90 yet covered only 4.6% of outcomes at one sigma versus 68% calibrated.
